Attention: Lauren Heath, Chief Operating Officer
Dear Ms. Heath,

We are glad to confirm that Ashcombe Advisory Partners will lead the investor relations program for {{fact:f:E-2018-001.client}}, and this letter sets out what the two firms have agreed so that we begin from the same understanding. It is a plain document by design; where the language is careful, that is to be clear rather than cautious. Please read it alongside the conversations of these past weeks, which it is meant to record and not to replace.
The program and how we will run it

Our charge is to help {{fact:f:E-2018-001.client}} be understood clearly by the investors, analysts, and reporters who follow the company, and to have it ready to speak in one voice whenever it has something to say. In practice that means shaping the core messages, drafting the announcements and supporting materials as they are needed, and standing with your team on the timing and sequencing of what goes out.

Most of the work will move by email and short calls, with the occasional working session when a decision needs the room. We will follow a plan we set together at the outset and revisit as the year unfolds, since an investor relations calendar rarely survives an earnings date untouched. Where a piece of work falls outside what we have scoped here, we will tell you before we begin it, not after.
Your team at Ashcombe

Michael Morris will lead the engagement day to day, and he will be your first call on strategy and on anything sensitive that wants a considered read. Laura Bradley will carry much of the drafting and keep the moving parts in order, and Michelle Black will manage the announcement timelines and the approvals that sit behind them.

I will stay close to the relationship myself. Any announcement that carries real consequence will have my own review before it leaves our hands, so that a partner has read it and not only signed for it.
How we will keep you informed

You will hear from us on a steady cadence rather than only when something is due, because an investor relations program suffers more from silence than from too much contact. Michael Morris will send a short written status at regular intervals and will always be reachable between them, and we will hold a working session whenever a decision is better made in conversation than in a thread. Each note we send will be tied to the specific piece of work it concerns, so the record stays easy to follow long after the fact.
What we will ask of you

An engagement like this works best when one person on your side can speak for the company on messaging, and we understand that person to be you. We will look to you for timely review of drafts, for early word on anything market-moving before it becomes public, and for access to the leaders whose words we help shape. In return we will keep our asks few and clear, and we will not let a missing approval be the reason an announcement slips.
Fee and commencement

We will begin on {{fact:f:E-2018-001.start}}, and the program is expected to run for roughly nine months from that date. Our fee for the work described above is {{fact:f:E-2018-001.fee}}, fixed for that scope, so that you can plan the year with confidence and call on us without watching a clock.
Fees and payment

The fee of {{fact:f:E-2018-001.fee}} covers the program as scoped and is billed in equal monthly installments across the term, each invoice payable within thirty days of its date. Out-of-pocket costs that we incur on your behalf, such as wire-service fees or print production, will be billed at cost and only with your prior agreement. Work you ask us to take on beyond the agreed scope will be quoted separately and started only once you have approved it.
Term and termination

The engagement runs for the period described above and continues until the program is complete or either firm ends it. Either of us may end it on thirty days' written notice, and you will owe fees only for work performed through the effective date of that notice. On request we will return or destroy your materials promptly and help hand off anything in progress, so that nothing is left stranded.
Confidentiality

We will treat the non-public information you share with us as confidential and use it only for the work you have engaged us to do. Our people are held to the same obligation, and we will not disclose your confidential information outside the firm without your consent, except where the law requires it and then only after we have told you, if we are permitted to. This duty outlasts the engagement itself.
Limitation of liability

We will perform our work with the care and skill you are entitled to expect of an advisor in our field. Our counsel supports your decisions and does not replace your own judgment or that of your legal, accounting, and other professional advisors, and responsibility for what the company says and does publicly remains with the company. To the extent the law allows, our liability arising out of this engagement is limited to the fees paid to us under it, and neither firm will be liable to the other for indirect or consequential losses.
Governing law

This letter and the engagement it describes are governed by the laws of the state in which our firm is organized, and we each agree to resolve any dispute there. Should any part of this letter be found unenforceable, the rest of it will stand.

If this letter reflects what we discussed, please sign below and return a copy to us, and we will be ready to begin on the date noted above. If anything here reads differently from your understanding, tell me and we will settle it before you sign. The next step is a signed copy back to my attention, and Michael Morris will follow that same week to set our kickoff.
With regards,
Kickoff Memo: Investor Relations Program for {{fact:f:E-2018-001.client}}
To: Laura Bradley, Michelle Black
From: Michael Morris
Re: Getting the engagement moving before the first drafts do

This is the investor relations program for {{fact:f:E-2018-001.client}}, and I want the three of us aligned on what we are trying to accomplish before any drafts start moving, because the work will go a good deal faster if we are building toward the same picture from the first week rather than reconciling three different pictures in the third. The company wants to be read clearly and consistently by the people who follow it, and our job over the next several months is to give them the messages, the materials, and the routine that make that happen without a scramble every time something has to go out.

We begin on {{fact:f:E-2018-001.start}}. An hour spent agreeing the shape of the work will spare us a tangle of mismatched drafts once things are moving, each built on a slightly different assumption about where this is headed, so I have set out below the lines of work as I see them and the first moves I am asking each of us to make.
The lines of work

items: 1. Message architecture. We pull together how the company is understood today, agree with the client how it wants to be understood, and write the core narrative and the handful of supporting messages that everything else will hang off.

2. Announcement support. We build the drafting and approval routine for the releases and investor materials the company will put out over the engagement, so that nothing reaches the market without the right people having read it in the right order.

3. Calendar and readiness. We map the company's known events for the period, mark the moments that will need messaging well ahead of time, and make sure we are never caught drafting something important against the clock.

4. Relationships and access. We fix the short list of people we will need time with on the client side, starting with Lauren Heath, so that reviews and sign-offs do not stall for want of the right person in the room.

blocks.text: These four lines do not run in parallel so much as feed one another, and the order matters: the message architecture comes first because almost everything downstream is built on it, the announcement routine and the calendar can stand up alongside it, and the access we need from the client is what keeps any of it from stalling. If we get the first line right and early, the rest of the engagement is mostly a matter of execution rather than argument.
The first two weeks
Here is what I need from each of us to start, and I have kept the list deliberately short so that we can actually clear it rather than admire it:

items: 1. Laura Bradley stands up the working file and a draft schedule for the message work and circulates a first cut by the end of next week.
2. Michelle Black builds the approvals tracker and confirms with the client's office who signs off on what, so we are not guessing when the first material is ready.
3. I run the opening call with Lauren Heath and bring back the company's own read on which audience matters most right now, which is the one input that shapes everything in the first line of work.

blocks.text: Send me anything I have missed by Friday. If I do not hear otherwise, we work to this, and we adjust it in the open as the engagement teaches us where it was wrong.
Hi Lauren,

I am opening this thread so that everything on the {{fact:f:E-2018-001.client}} investor relations program stays in one place and easy to find, and I have copied my colleagues so that we are all working from the same messages as the engagement gets underway. On our side, Laura Bradley will handle much of the drafting and keep the schedule straight, and Michelle Black will run the approval timelines so that nothing you need to see reaches you late or out of order. For the file, our point of contact with your office is you, Lauren Heath, and yours with us is me.

We have made a start on the message work, and I expect a first cut of the core narrative to you within the next couple of weeks. Before that draft hardens, one read from you would help us more than anything else at this stage: which audience we should lead with, since the investor story and the wider market story do not always want the same opening.
If it is easier to talk that through than to write it out, send me two or three windows and I will set a short call; otherwise a line back is plenty and we will build from there.
Sincerely

blocks.text: Meeting Minutes: Investor Relations Program for {{fact:f:E-2018-001.client}}
These are the notes from our working session on the {{fact:f:E-2018-001.client}} program. We met to take stock at the midpoint and to line up the second half of the work.
Present

items: Michael Morris, Partner, Ashcombe Advisory Partners
Laura Bradley, Senior Associate, Ashcombe Advisory Partners
Michelle Black, Communications Analyst, Ashcombe Advisory Partners
Lauren Heath, Chief Operating Officer, {{fact:f:E-2018-001.client}}

blocks.text: What we covered

Michael Morris opened with a look back at the first half. The core narrative is written. It is with the client for comment now. We agreed the story is holding up well, and that the three pillars underneath it are carrying their weight.

We went through the pillars one at a time. Each is meant to stand on a proof point, not on an adjective. Two of them are strong. The third leans a little hard on language and not enough on evidence. Laura Bradley took the note to find a firmer fact to sit it on.

Lauren Heath gave us her read from the client side. Leadership likes the direction. A few lines still need softening for an investor audience, and one claim reads stronger than the company is ready to stand behind in public. She will send those notes back to us marked on the draft, so nothing gets lost in translation.

Then we turned to the second half. The plan is to build the working materials off the agreed narrative, one at a time, rather than all at once. Mike asked Laura Bradley to take the first pass at the investor Q&A, since that is where the softening will matter most. I will keep the approvals tracker current, so we always know who owes a sign-off and when a window closes.

We talked about the website and the templates as well. Those come later in the plan. But we want the language there to match the narrative once it is locked, so we noted it now and left it parked. Nobody starts on it until the core story is settled.

We spent a little time on the announcement calendar. There is nothing urgent in the near term. We agreed to keep testing each new message against the calendar as we go, so a live announcement never catches us with the wrong words ready. Michael Morris reminded us to keep the client close on anything market-facing, and to hear about it early rather than late.
What we agreed to do

rows: Return the marked-up narrative with the investor-audience notes
First draft of the investor Q&A off the agreed narrative
Keep the approvals tracker current and flag any stalled sign-off
Set the review and confirm the sequence for the second-half materials

Status Report: Investor Relations Program for {{fact:f:E-2018-001.client}}

rows: Michael Morris, Partner, Ashcombe Advisory Partners

blocks.text: Where the program stands

We have reached the midpoint of the investor relations program for {{fact:f:E-2018-001.client}}, and I am glad to report that the work is on plan and the budget is tracking with it. The first half was about getting the story right before we spent effort on the materials that carry it, on the reasoning that a message architecture is only as sound as the reading of the market it rests on, and a shaky reading grows expensive to correct once everything else has been built on top of it. That reading is done, the core narrative is written, and it is with your team for comment, which is exactly where I hoped we would be at this point in the calendar. What follows sets out what the last period produced, the work ahead, where the fee sits against the plan, and the handful of risks I am tracking.
What we completed this period

Most of the first half went into evidence and drafting, so that the positioning rests on how the company is actually read and not on how we would prefer it to be read. The work broke down into four pieces, and all four are in hand:

items: 1. A positioning review of the company's public materials and the last two years of its announcements, with the gaps and the mixed signals marked.
2. Listening sessions with your leadership and with analysts who cover the sector, pulled together into the themes that shape how the company is understood today.
3. A message architecture of one core narrative and three supporting messages, each carried by concrete proof points rather than adjectives, which Laura Bradley drafted in the company's own register.
4. An approvals routine, stood up by Michelle Black, that tracks who owes a sign-off and when a window closes, so no material reaches the market out of order.

blocks.text: The work ahead

The second half turns the agreed narrative into the things your people reach for day to day, and it does so one piece at a time so that quality does not slip as the materials multiply. Once your comments on the draft are in, we lock the core story and build outward from it:

items: 1. Draft the working materials off the locked narrative: the standard boilerplate, an executive Q&A for the harder questions, and briefing notes for the next round of investor conversations.
2. Refresh the language on the website and in your templates so that every place the company speaks carries the same story.
3. Run a short session with your spokespeople so that the people who actually talk to investors and the press are using the agreed language and not their own.

blocks.text: The budget

The engagement is tracking within its fixed fee of {{fact:f:E-2018-001.fee}}, and the first half came in on the effort we scoped, so I do not see anything in the work ahead that pushes past it. If a request comes up that sits outside what we agreed, such as materials for an event that was not in the original plan, I will flag it and price it with you before the work starts and not once it is done.
Risks I am tracking
Three things are worth naming now, while each is still small enough to manage, and none of them threatens the engagement:

items: 1. Sign-off on the narrative. Everything in the second half builds on the core story, so a delay in your team's comments moves the later work with it; I have asked for those notes by the review already on the calendar.

2. One voice to the market. Several people at the company speak to investors and the press, and the positioning only holds if they use the same language, which is what the Q&A and the spokesperson session are built to secure.

3. A live announcement in the window. If a result or a transaction lands mid-engagement, we will want to test the new messaging against it before anything goes public, so keeping me in the loop early on anything market-facing gives us the room to do that.

blocks.text: The one thing I need from you next is your team's comments on the core narrative draft. With those in hand the second half moves quickly, and Laura Bradley and I will have the marked-up narrative ready for the review we already have on the calendar.
